groups.text: When you fill in a paper form, you don't write the form's name in every box.
You are already holding it.
A Java builder lambda gets the builder as a parameter, b, and names it on every line.
Kotlin can hand the builder to the lambda as its receiver.
Inside the braces, the builder is this.
So the calls need no prefix, as if you were writing a method of the builder itself.
One level down, nothing magic happens.
A lambda with receiver has the same type as a lambda that takes the builder as its first argument.
Both compile to a Functionone.
Only the compiler treats that first argument as this.
Builders nest. Inside paymentRequest, the payer block hands you a second builder, a PartyBuilder.
Now two receivers are in scope, one inside the other.
A bare call goes to the nearest receiver that has it.
Name lands on the party.
Now someone types payee inside payer, by mistake.
The PartyBuilder has no payee.
What does Kotlin do?
It keeps looking, outward.
The outer builder has payee, so the line compiles.
And it quietly builds a second party.
In the lesson's demo it fails only when it runs: iban required for oops.
Without a required field, you would simply send the wrong request.
The fix is one annotation.
Mark an annotation class with @DslMarker, and put it on every builder class: the receivers themselves.
Now only the nearest marked receiver is implicit.
The misplaced payee stops at the inner wall.
It no longer compiles.
You can still reach the outer builder on purpose, with a label: this@paymentRequest.currency.
Nobody types that by accident.
In Kotlin that is the whole fix: one marker annotation, placed on each builder class.
Java needs none of it.
Its lambdas name every builder, so reaching the outer one means typing r on purpose.
The rule: a bare call goes to the nearest receiver that has it, and @DslMarker on the builder classes stops it there.
A quick check.
Inside payer, someone writes currency equals GBP, with no label.
With the marker on, does it compile?
